title: Dolores County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Dolores County wells run about 150 ft deep with a 7 gpm median yield. Learn what that means for drilling cost and water supply.
h1: Water wells in Dolores County, Colorado
intro_html:
Dolores County is classic mountain fractured-bedrock country, with most wells tapping unnamed bedrock aquifers and a few into the Dakota and Morrison formations. Records from 597 permitted wells give a decent picture of how deep drillers go, how much water they usually find, and what that tends to cost.

If you are looking at land outside places like Dove Creek or Rico, it pays to understand the spread in well depths, the range of yields, and the local drilling history before you budget or make an offer.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Dolores County
sections.html:
Across Dolores County, the median well depth is 150 feet, with the middle half between 82 and 245 feet. That means most drilling bids will be built around that range, but there are outliers. About 29% of wells stop under 100 feet, while 62% land between 100 and 300 feet. A smaller share go deeper, with 6% between 300 and 600 feet and 3% over 600 feet. The deepest well on record reaches 1,220 feet.

In fractured mountain bedrock, a driller often has to chase water-bearing fractures rather than a flat water table, so two neighbors can have very different depths. Plan your budget around something in the middle, but know the rock can force you deeper.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water you usually get
sections.html:
Reported pumping rates in Dolores County look reasonably solid for household use. The median yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half of wells fall between 3.2 and 11.0 gpm. About 49% of wells report between 5 and 15 gpm, and another 19% are over 15 gpm, which is generous for single-family use.

The low end matters too. Roughly 27% of wells come in between 1 and 5 gpm, and 5% report under 1 gpm. In Colorado, even a 1–2 gpm well can work with storage, but those sub‑1 gpm wells are borderline and may need careful management or augmentation planning if you are trying to do more than basic household and allowed stock use.

sections.heading: Depth to water and what that means
sections.html:
Only a subset of Dolores County wells report static water level, but the pattern is clear enough to plan around. The median depth to water is 60 feet below ground, with the middle half of measurements between 30 and 103 feet. That means many wells have a good column of water above the pump, even when the total depth is much greater.

In fractured-bedrock settings, water level can be more about local fractures than a smooth “water table,” so you cannot assume your lot matches a neighbor’s reading. Still, knowing that most measured wells hit water within about the first 100 feet helps size pumps and storage and gives you a sense of typical drawdown margins under normal household pumping.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and permit history
sections.html:
Dolores County’s well records go back to a single permit in the 1950s, then pick up from 8 in the 1960s to 39 in the 1970s and 50 in the 1980s. Drilling really increased in the 1990s with 107 permits, and peaked in the 2000s with 146. Activity stayed steady afterwards, with 73 permits in the 2010s and 49 already in the 2020s, up through a newest permit year of 2025.

Most wells are for domestic or household use (72%), with stock wells making up 18%, monitoring wells 8%, and irrigation about 2%. The work has been dominated by mountain outfits like Mcpherson Drilling Co. (138 wells), Ucolo Drilling Llc (59), and Kilby'S Water Well Service (19), all experienced in fractured-bedrock drilling.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost
sections.html:
Here the ground is mainly fractured granite and gneiss, so drillers charge mountain-bedrock rates. The typical drilling rate runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 150-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole itself in the ballpark of $9,800–$15,000.

When you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished well at that median depth generally lands around $15,800–$27,000. Shallower wells from the under‑100‑foot group tend to come in below that range, while the 300‑plus‑foot jobs can run higher. When you get a bid, make sure the per‑foot rate, materials, and an allowance for pump size and trench length are spelled out clearly.

sections.heading: Local risks: low yield, dry holes, and contamination
sections.html:
With only 5% of reported wells under 1 gpm, true “trickle” producers are not common here, but they do exist. In fractured bedrock, that usually means the borehole missed major fractures. Before you buy, review nearby permits for depth and yield so you know if you’re in a strong pocket or a marginal one. The 3% of wells over 600 feet show what can happen when drillers have to keep chasing water.

Environmental mapping shows about 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 8 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site within roughly 10 miles. That doesn’t mean your water is bad, but it does mean you should test a new or existing well thoroughly for metals and industrial contaminants, not just basic potability, and plan your septic layout to keep good separation from the well.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in Dolores County
sections.html:
For a rural lot in Dolores County or near nearby counties like Montezuma or San Miguel, your first homework is around water. Look up surrounding wells: most are 100–300 feet deep with a 7.0 gpm median yield, but there is enough spread that you should not rely on averages alone. Confirm whether you will have a domestic exempt well, a stock well, or something tied to irrigation or monitoring, and make sure the allowed uses match your plans.

Budget realistically based on the median 150‑foot depth, but keep a contingency for drilling deeper. For existing homes, pull the original permit and any pump test data, then order a full water-quality panel. Tie your driveway, house site, well location, and septic layout together early so you don’t paint yourself into a corner with setbacks and trench runs.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Dolores County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Dolores County, the median well depth is 150 feet, and the middle half of wells fall between 82 and 245 feet. About 29% are under 100 feet, while 62% are between 100 and 300 feet. Only a small share go deeper, with 6% between 300 and 600 feet and 3% over 600 feet. The deepest well on record reaches 1,220 feet.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Dolores County?
faq.a: Reported wells in Dolores County show a median pump yield of 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half of wells between 3.2 and 11.0 gpm. Around 49% produce 5–15 gpm and 19% are above 15 gpm. On the low side, 27% report 1–5 gpm and 5% are under 1 gpm, which may require careful management and storage for reliable use.

faq.q: How deep is the water table in Dolores County?
faq.a: Static water level reports are limited, but the data available indicate a median depth to water of 60 feet below ground, with the middle half between 30 and 103 feet. In fractured-bedrock settings like Dolores County, water levels can vary a lot over short distances, so you should treat these numbers as general guidance and check nearby wells for more site-specific expectations.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a water well in Dolores County?
faq.a: In Dolores County’s fractured mountain bedrock, drillers usually charge about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 150-foot median depth, that puts the drilling portion roughly in the $9,800–$15,000 range. When you include casing, pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, a complete well at that depth commonly totals about $15,800–$27,000, with shallower or deeper wells coming in below or above that range.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Dolores County, Colorado?
faq.a: Water quality varies by location. Records show about 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 8 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site within roughly 10 miles. Those do not automatically affect your well, but they are enough reason to test thoroughly. For any existing or new well, plan on a full lab analysis for bacteria, metals, and industrial contaminants before relying on it for drinking.
